review_basis: Visually inspected original AWS AIP Module 03 slide images 28–33 from site-ready archives; narration follows concrete policy, telemetry and scoring illustrations.
part_title: AgentCore Policy Enforcement, Evaluations and Observability

scenes.title: Policy in AgentCore
scenes.narration: This slide introduces a policy decision before an agent is allowed to execute a sensitive tool. The agent proposes a refund for order forty-two in the amount of one hundred twenty dollars. That request reaches AgentCore Gateway and a policy evaluation step. Follow the arrow into the Cedar policy box. The business rule permits refunds without manager approval only up to one hundred dollars. Because the proposed amount is one hundred twenty and manager approval is false, the decision is deny. The red branch on the right shows that the refund tool is not executed. This is the difference between asking the model to follow a policy and enforcing that policy outside the model. The model can suggest an action, but a deterministic authorization layer decides whether it may proceed. Read the closing line: approved calls can proceed when the policy explicitly permits them. Always distinguish authorization from tool success; an allowed refund can still fail for a separate operational reason.

scenes.title: Policy Enforcement
scenes.narration: The next slide makes the default-deny policy model more explicit. A proposed tool call arrives with a user claim of finance, an action of make_payment, and an amount of one hundred twenty. The decision table on the left shows that a finance user may make a payment up to one hundred, but a higher amount is denied. Other roles and actions are denied unless a rule explicitly permits them. The central gateway policy engine applies those conditions. The green route forwards a permitted operation to its tool, while the red route blocks a denied request. Look at the two modes at the bottom. Enforce mode actually blocks calls based on the decision. Log-only mode records the decision for testing but lets the tool call continue. That difference is critical during rollout. Log-only helps observe the potential impact of a policy, but it should not be confused with protection. Move to enforcement only after validating policy rules, test scenarios and legitimate business workflows.

scenes.title: AgentCore Evaluations
scenes.narration: This slide introduces systematic evaluation of agent behavior. On the left, the inputs include the user's request, agent traces and task outputs. The middle evaluators score goal completion, tool choice, response quality and difficult edge cases. On the right, CloudWatch Observability Insights aggregates scores and trends, allowing teams to identify recurring problems and decide what to improve. The bottom example demonstrates why evaluating the final answer alone is insufficient. A travel assistant is asked for the weather in Paris, but the agent calls a calendar tool. Even if it produces plausible language, the wrong tool choice is an observable failure. The illustrative tool-selection score is low because a weather tool would have been relevant. Evaluations can inform alerts, prompt changes, tool-description improvements and regression tests. They do not automatically fix the problem. Choose representative evaluation cases and investigate traces so the score connects to an actionable defect.

scenes.title: Reading AgentCore Observability
scenes.narration: This diagram turns telemetry into a debugging exercise. Look at the three charts across the top. The goal success rate drops after noon; p95 latency increases; and the error rate spikes around the same period. Those related changes suggest a real operational problem rather than isolated noise. The lower-left timeline traces one agent request through the user message, the agent, and two tool calls. An annotation highlights a wrong tool selection, where the agent invokes GetOrderStatus instead of SearchCatalog. On the right, evaluator scores show that more traces are receiving low marks. The bottom row gives a three-step investigation: identify the pattern in metrics, correlate it with actual tool traces, and then review evaluator output and tool input/output details to identify the cause. The charts are illustrative, not live production screenshots. The engineering lesson is to use metrics, traces and evaluator scores together, rather than guessing from one aggregate graph.

scenes.title: Built-In Evaluation Dimensions
scenes.narration: This slide shows an important limitation of fluent language. On the left, a user asks a question about a travel policy and the assistant responds with a clear-sounding statement that a hotel has a certain reimbursement limit. The red warning points out that the number is not supported by the supplied source documents. The scorecard on the right evaluates several independent dimensions: factual correctness and faithfulness to the source, helpfulness, instruction following, tool choice and parameter accuracy, safety, and goal success. An answer can pass tone and helpfulness checks while failing source faithfulness and goal completion. The far-right column also shows that evaluations can run on selected sessions or sampled traces, with filters and defined subjects. Evaluation quality depends on the cases and evidence selected. When auditing a RAG or agent application, require the model to ground factual claims in the actual retrieved policy rather than rewarding an attractive but unsupported answer.

scenes.title: Custom Evaluators
scenes.narration: When built-in quality dimensions do not fully express your business requirements, you can define custom evaluation criteria. The six steps across the top show the workflow. Select a judge model, write a rubric prompt, choose a scoring scale, decide whether to evaluate an entire session, trace or specific tool call, and run the evaluator against saved outputs. Finally, inspect scores and example explanations. The lower panel contains a concrete rubric: was the selected tool appropriate for the user's request? The example asks for weather in Seattle, but the agent invokes a calendar tool. The judge assigns a low score and explains why that selection is mostly inappropriate. Notice the one-to-five scale and the example result of two out of five. Custom rubrics should have clear definitions, representative negative and positive cases, and regular calibration. An LLM judge can also make mistakes, so compare its judgments with independent human or deterministic checks when consequences are significant.
